passages.happening:
“Therefore, since Christ suffered in His body, arm yourselves with the same resolve, because anyone who has suffered in his body is done with sin. Consequently, he does not live out his remaining time on earth for human passions, but for the will of God” (verses 1-2).

“For you have spent enough time in the past carrying out the same desires as the Gentiles: living in debauchery, lust, drunkenness, orgies, carousing, and detestable idolatry. Because of this, they consider it strange of you not to plunge with them into the same flood of reckless indiscretion, and they heap abuse on you. But they will have to give an account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead” (verses 3-5).

“That is why the gospel was preached even to those who are now dead, so that they might be judged as men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 3 ended with Christ on his throne after suffering. ‘Therefore’: those who belong to him should take up the same resolve. ‘Arm yourselves’ is a soldier's word. The resolve is a weapon.

‘Anyone who has suffered in his body is done with sin’ is a hard line. Verse 2 explains what Peter means: such a person no longer spends the rest of life on human passions, but on the will of God. He has made a break. Peter is not saying that suffering makes anyone sinless.

Then Peter names the old life plainly. The list describes ordinary social life in a Greek or Roman town: drinking parties, sexual licence, and above all the feasts and festivals in honour of the gods. Those feasts were also where people belonged, did business and kept up friendships in their trade. When a convert stopped going, it looked strange, ungrateful, even disloyal to the city and its gods. So old friends turned on them: ‘they heap abuse on you’.

‘Flood of reckless indiscretion’ pictures a rushing tide of excess that everyone else was plunging into together.

Peter's answer is not to fight back. It is to remember that every person will give an account to God, the judge of ‘the living and the dead’. The mockers are not the final court.

Verse 6 is hard (see below). Its plain point is that death does not defeat the gospel.
passages.ot:
The prophets warned against the drinking feasts of the careless: “Woe to those who rise early in the morning in pursuit of strong drink, who linger into the evening, to be inflamed by wine” (Isaiah 5:11).

And the Bible often speaks of God as judge of all: “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (Genesis 18:25).
passages.hard:
Verse 6 says the gospel was ‘preached even to those who are now dead’. Does this mean people can hear the gospel after death?

Readers take the verse in two main ways. These notes do not choose. Many take it to mean that the gospel was preached to believers during their lives, who have since died. Pagan neighbours may have mocked that Christians die like everyone else. Peter answers that though they were ‘judged’ in the flesh, they died, perhaps even condemned by others, they will live before God. The word ‘now’ in the BSB's ‘those who are now dead’ reflects this reading.

Others link the verse with 3:19 and read it of Christ's proclamation to the dead between his death and resurrection. Some in the early church and since have drawn from it a hope for those who died without hearing the gospel. Most Christian traditions have been careful not to build a teaching of a second chance after death on this one verse, since its meaning is uncertain, and they differ over what hope may be held for those who never heard.

These notes say no more than the text does about anyone's state after death. Peter's own point is pastoral: death does not defeat the gospel, and those who suffered for Christ are not lost.
passages.asks: Ask what ‘human passions’ still set the direction of your time. Ask whether your old friends have found you ‘strange’, and how you have answered them. And ask whether you live as one who will give an account, and who trusts God with the account others will give.

passages.happening:
“The end of all things is near. Therefore be clear-minded and sober, so that you can pray. Above all, love one another deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without complaining” (verses 7-9).

“As good stewards of the manifold grace of God, each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another. If anyone speaks, he should speak as one conveying the words of God. If anyone serves, he should serve with the strength God provides, so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen” (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
‘The end of all things is near.’ Peter does not give a date. He draws a conclusion: be clear-headed, so that you can pray. The nearness of the end does not make believers frantic. It makes them sober, prayerful, and loving.

‘Above all, love one another deeply.’ The reason: ‘love covers over a multitude of sins’. In a small community under pressure, people rub each other the wrong way. Love does not keep score. It covers.

Then hospitality. Believers travelled for work and ministry, and inns were unsafe or of bad reputation. Churches met in homes. So opening your home was a constant and costly service. That is why Peter adds ‘without complaining’.

Then gifts. Each believer has received a gift of grace. A ‘steward’ was a household manager, often a trusted slave, who handled the master's goods on his behalf. Gifts belong to God and are held in trust for others. Peter sorts them into two broad kinds: speaking and serving. Whoever speaks should speak as one carrying God's words. Whoever serves should serve in God's strength. And the goal of it all is that God be glorified through Jesus Christ.

The section ends with praise and ‘Amen’. The long part of the letter on living among outsiders, which began at 2:11, closes here.
passages.ot:
‘Love covers over a multitude of sins’ comes from Proverbs: “Hatred stirs up dissension, but love covers all transgressions” (Proverbs 10:12).

Abraham's welcome of three strangers is the Bible's great picture of hospitality: “Let a little water be brought, that you may wash your feet and rest yourselves under the tree. And I will bring a bit of bread so that you may refresh yourselves” (Genesis 18:4-5).

And the law told Israel to open its hand to the needy: “Instead, you are to open your hand to him and freely loan him whatever he needs” (Deuteronomy 15:8).
passages.asks: Ask whom you find hard to love in your church, and whether love could cover what you have been keeping score of. Ask when you last opened your home without complaining. And ask what gift God has given you, and whom it is meant to serve.

passages.happening:
“Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial that has come upon you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may be overjoyed at the revelation of His glory. If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you” (verses 12-14).

“Indeed, none of you should suffer as a murderer or thief or wrongdoer, or even as a meddler. But if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but glorify God that you bear that name” (verses 15-16).

“For it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God; and if it begins with us, what will the outcome be for those who disobey the gospel of God? And, ‘If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?’ So then, those who suffer according to God’s will should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good” (verses 17-19).
passages.hearers:
‘Beloved’ opens a new section, as at 2:11. Peter returns to suffering, now with the word ‘fiery’. It recalls the fire that tests gold in 1:7. The trial is painful, but it is not strange. Christ suffered too.

‘Rejoice’ does not mean pretend. It means that sharing Christ's sufferings joins you to him, and those who share his sufferings will share his glory. When they are insulted for his name, ‘the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you’.

Verse 16 holds one of only three uses of the name ‘Christian’ in the New Testament. It was probably first given by outsiders, meaning followers of Christ, and it could be said with contempt. Within a few decades the name itself could bring legal danger. The Roman historian Tacitus reports that Nero blamed the Christians for the great fire of Rome in AD 64 and had many put to death. Around AD 110 to 112 Pliny, governor of Bithynia and Pontus, two of the very provinces this letter went to, asked the emperor whether people should be punished for the name alone. Scholars differ over which of these settings, if any, the letter's ‘fiery trial’ reflects.

Peter draws a line. Suffer for being a Christian, and do not be ashamed. But do not suffer for doing wrong. ‘Meddler’ is a rare word, perhaps for someone who interferes in other people's business. Even a good cause does not license that.

‘Judgment to begin with the family of God’ most likely means the refining that God's people go through now, in suffering. If even this is hard, Peter says, how serious is the outcome for those who refuse the gospel.

And the last word is trust. ‘Entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good.’ The Creator who made them has not stopped caring for them.
passages.ot:
Peter quotes Proverbs 11:31 in its Greek form: “If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?” (verse 18). The BSB of Proverbs reads, “If the righteous receive their due on earth, how much more the ungodly and the sinner!” (Proverbs 11:31).

Judgment beginning with God's own people is an old prophetic theme. In Ezekiel's vision God says, “Now begin at My sanctuary” (Ezekiel 9:6). And the refiner's fire is in Malachi: “For He will be like a refiner’s fire” (Malachi 3:2).

‘The Spirit of glory’ echoes Isaiah's promise of the Messiah: “The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him” (Isaiah 11:2). And ‘entrust their souls’ echoes the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross: “Into Your hands I commit my spirit” (Psalm 31:5).
passages.hard:
Is suffering God's judgment on the one who suffers? And what should someone do in a ‘fiery trial’?

Peter does not say that a person's suffering is God's punishment. He speaks of believers suffering for doing good and for bearing Christ's name, and he calls it sharing in Christ's sufferings. ‘Judgment beginning with the family of God’ is about God refining his people, not condemning them. These verses must never be used to tell someone in pain that God is against them.

Nor do they tell anyone to suffer alone or in silence. ‘Entrust’ is trust, not isolation, and the same chapter surrounds sufferers with a praying, loving, hospitable church.

Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whether you have been surprised by hardship, as if following Christ should have spared you. Ask whether you have ever been ashamed of his name. And ask what it would look like this week to entrust yourself to your faithful Creator and keep doing good.
